error_modes.label: GROUND SEGMENT OF THE FORMATION MISSION PLANNING AND BRIEFING

texts.0: SP, due to mission planning built without identifying the threats specific to a two-ship ground operation, did not plan the sortie according to aircraft energy planning and left the ground segment of the formation briefing uncovered. Check-in times, start sequence, taxi order, radio frequency plan and the spare aircraft procedure were all undefined, and the alternate mission was not planned. IP had to rebuild the ground plan and dictate every timing before the flight was allowed to step to the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to planning taken from the previous sortie without checking it against the day's tasking, did not take into consideration the delayed start time and did not brief the ground abort and spare procedure. Each missing ground item was covered only after IP prompted for it in turn, and the alternate mission was left in outline. The ground plan reached the lower limit of the standard purely on verbal prompting and put the flight about ten minutes behind the briefed step time.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete threat review at the start of planning, initially omitted the taxi route restriction published for the day from the ground portion of the brief. SP identified the omission while reviewing the planning sheets, rebriefed the taxi order and the affected holding point, and adjusted the start time accordingly, without IP intervention. The flight stepped on time with the ground plan complete.
texts.3: SP planned the ground segment of the formation sortie suitably, according to aircraft energy planning and own training level, and took part in the briefing according to the Mission Briefing Guide. Check-in times, start and taxi sequence, frequency plan, ground abort criteria and the spare aircraft procedure were all covered and consistent with the tasking. No item required correction by IP.
texts.4: SP produced a ground plan of exceptional quality, with start, check-in and taxi timings computed to the minute and cross-checked against Local Area Procedures and the day's field conditions. Every ground contingency raised in the brief, including the loss of the leader and the spare aircraft changeover, was already supported by a prepared procedure. Departures from the ideal plan were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP planned and briefed the ground segment within standards, but the ground abort and spare aircraft procedures were stated as headings rather than as decisions for this specific sortie. The trend is toward a plan that satisfies the briefing guide while leaving the flight without an agreed course of action if a ground problem occurs. SP is expected to brief each ground contingency against the actual timings, parking layout and aircraft availability on the next event.

error_modes.label: STANDARD TAXI DISTANCE FROM THE LEADER AS NUMBER TWO

texts.0: SP, due to taxi power applied in large steps instead of a steady setting matched to the leader, did not keep the standard distance from the leader during taxi. SP closed to well inside one aircraft length behind the leader on the taxiway and then dropped back far enough to lose the leader's turn onto the holding point. IP took the controls to re-establish the interval and stop the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the cockpit instead of on the leader's aircraft, did not maintain the standard distance during taxi and allowed the interval to shrink to the minimum acceptable spacing behind the leader. The interval was restored only after IP called for more spacing on two separate occasions. Distance stayed at the limit of the standard for the remainder of the taxi and no jet blast margin was preserved at the run-up position.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction after the first taxiway turn, initially allowed the distance from the leader to reduce below the standard spacing. SP recognized the closure, reduced power and used brakes progressively, and re-established the briefed interval before the next turn, without IP intervention. Distance from the leader remained within the standard for the rest of the taxi.
texts.3: SP kept the standard distance from the leader throughout taxi as Number Two, holding the briefed interval steadily through turns, the run-up position and the line-up. Spacing was maintained with smooth power and brake use and preserved jet blast and wingtip clearance at all times. No correction was required from the leader or from IP.
texts.4: SP held the standard taxi distance from the leader with exceptional precision, keeping the briefed interval essentially constant through every turn, stop and power change of the leader. Spacing was adjusted in anticipation of the leader's actions rather than in reaction to them, and clearance from obstacles and other aircraft was preserved without any need for the leader to adjust taxi speed. Variations from the briefed interval were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the distance from the leader within standards, but the interval was held at the close end throughout the taxi and was maintained by repeated brake application rather than by a steady power setting. The trend is toward a spacing that leaves no margin for a sudden stop by the leader on a congested taxiway. SP is expected to select an interval nearer the briefed value and control it with power on the next sortie.

texts.0: SP, due to the radio panel being set from memory instead of from the briefed frequency plan, did not execute the frequency checks on the ground before taxi. SP was on the wrong frequency at the leader's check-in, missed the check-in call entirely and did not answer the subsequent calls. IP had to set the correct frequency, check in on behalf of the flight and delay taxi until two-way contact was confirmed.
texts.1: SP, due to the frequency check being started only after the leader's first call, did not execute the check timely before taxi and answered the check-in late and with an incorrect call sign format. The correct frequency and the correct response were achieved only after IP pointed out both errors on the interphone. The flight checked in at the limit of the standard and taxi was delayed while the leader repeated the call.
texts.2: SP, due to a frequency selected one channel off the briefed setting, initially failed to hear the leader's ground check. SP recognized the error, reset the frequency from the pre-flight briefing card and answered the repeated check-in correctly and in the standard format, without IP intervention. All remaining ground frequency checks were executed timely and correctly.
texts.3: SP executed the frequency checks on the ground before taxi timely and correctly, without any IP intervention and exactly according to the pre-flight briefing. All radios were set to the briefed frequencies before the leader's call, and each check-in was answered in the correct sequence and standard format. The flight was ready to taxi at the briefed time.
texts.4: SP executed the ground frequency checks with exceptional accuracy, with primary and back-up frequencies set and verified ahead of the schedule established in the pre-flight briefing. Every check-in was answered immediately, in the correct order and with faultless phraseology, and SP confirmed the back-up frequency plan with the leader before taxi. Deviations from the briefed radio plan were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP executed the ground frequency checks correctly, but each response was delivered only after a noticeable delay and the back-up frequencies were left unset until after the check-in was complete. The trend is toward a radio setup that works when everything goes as briefed but is not ready for a frequency change on the ground. SP is expected to set and verify both primary and back-up frequencies before the leader's first call on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: CHECKLIST DISCIPLINE AND START SEQUENCE TIMING WITHIN THE FLIGHT

texts.0: SP, due to the checklist being run from memory in order to catch up with the leader's start time, did not execute the checks according to check list and skipped procedures required by Local Area Procedures and SOPs. The before-start and after-start checks were left incomplete and one item was actioned out of sequence with the leader. IP had to stop the sequence, restart the checklist from the beginning and take over the coordination with the leader.
texts.1: SP, due to time pressure created by a late strap-in, did not execute the checks in the standardized manner and omitted two after-start items while trying to match the leader's timing. Both omissions were recovered only after IP called each item on the interphone. The checks were completed at the lower limit of the standard and the flight taxied about five minutes behind the briefed time.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption from the ground crew during the before-taxi checks, initially skipped one checklist item and continued to the next section. SP detected the gap at the sequence break, returned to the missed item and completed the check list in the prescribed order, without IP intervention. The aircraft was ready in time for the leader's taxi call.
texts.3: SP executed all checks according to check list, without IP intervention, in an impeccable and standardized manner and did not skip any procedure required by Local Area Procedures and SOPs. The start and after-start sequence was completed in step with the leader and the aircraft was ready at the briefed time. No item required prompting.
texts.4: SP executed the checklist to an exceptional standard, completing every check in the prescribed order and pace while remaining exactly in step with the leader's start and taxi sequence. Each response was made against the actual indication rather than from expectation, and the aircraft was configured and ready ahead of the briefed time without any item being rushed. Departures from the standardized flow were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP executed the checks within standards, but the flow accelerated noticeably whenever the leader moved ahead in the sequence, and several responses were given before the corresponding indication was actually read. The trend is toward pacing the checklist against the leader instead of against the aircraft. SP is expected to hold a constant checklist pace and use the radio to coordinate any timing difference with the leader on the next event.

error_modes.label: RADIO DISCIPLINE AND RESPONSE TO LEADER VISUAL SIGNALS ON THE GROUND

texts.0: SP, due to the use of non-standard phraseology in place of the briefed formation calls, did not respond correctly to the leader's ground transmissions and misread the run-up signal as a taxi signal. SP advanced the throttle with the aircraft not aligned and the ground crew still moving in front of the wing. IP intervened on the controls and on the radio to stop the aircraft and re-establish the sequence with the leader.
texts.1: SP, due to transmissions made in plain language instead of the briefed formation phraseology, acknowledged the leader's ground calls late and with information the leader had not asked for. The correct format and the correct visual signal responses were achieved only after IP corrected the phraseology twice on the interphone. Coordination with the leader stayed at the lower limit of the standard through the run-up and line-up.
texts.2: SP, due to a first acknowledgement made with the wrong call sign, initially broke the standard formation phraseology on the ground frequency. SP corrected the call sign immediately, resumed the briefed format and read every subsequent visual signal from the leader correctly and on time, without IP intervention. Ground coordination with the leader was standard for the remainder of the sequence.
texts.3: SP used the standard formation phraseology on the ground throughout, acknowledged every leader transmission promptly and in the correct sequence, and responded correctly to each visual signal given by the leader. Run-up, line-up and hold signals were read and returned without hesitation and exactly as agreed in the pre-flight briefing. No clarification was needed from the leader or from IP.
texts.4: SP maintained exceptional radio and signal discipline on the ground, with every acknowledgement made in standard phraseology at the first call and every visual signal from the leader recognized and returned without delay. SP also confirmed the one ambiguous signal with a concise standard call before acting on it. Departures from the briefed communication plan were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept ground radio discipline within standards, but several acknowledgements carried extra wording beyond the briefed format and one visual signal was returned only after a second look at the leader. The trend is toward communication that remains understandable but adds length and delay on a busy ground frequency. SP is expected to use the exact briefed phraseology and to read the leader's signals at the first presentation on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: GROUND CREW COORDINATION AND CLEARANCE BEFORE SWITCH OR CONTROL MOVEMENT

texts.0: SP, due to a complete lack of communication with the ground crew while attention was directed at the leader's aircraft, did not establish the position of the marshaller before activating switches and moving the controls. SP moved the flight controls and released the brakes while a crew member was still working under the wing and no clearance had been received. IP intervened to stop the aircraft and re-establish contact with the ground crew.
texts.1: SP, due to hand signals given without confirming that the marshaller had seen them, allowed a mis-apprehension with the ground crew about the readiness of the aircraft for chocks removal. The confusion was resolved only after IP repeated the signals and clarified the sequence with the crew. Coordination reached the lower limit of the standard and the flight was held for about three minutes at the parking position.
texts.2: SP, due to a signal given before the marshaller had moved clear of the wing line, initially created a doubt in the ground crew about the intended action. SP stopped, re-established eye contact and repeated the signal in the standard sequence before any switch or control was moved, without IP intervention. The remaining coordination with the ground crew was carried out without mis-apprehension.
texts.3: SP cooperated with the ground crew throughout the ground phase without allowing any mis-apprehension, and was aware of the crew's position before activating any switch or moving any aircraft control. Every signal was given in the standard sequence and acknowledged before the corresponding action was taken. No intervention by IP or by the leader was required.
texts.4: SP coordinated with the ground crew to an exceptional standard, confirming the position of every crew member before each switch activation and control movement and keeping the signal exchange unambiguous throughout the start and chocks sequence. SP also passed the leader's timing changes to the crew so that both aircraft were released together. Any imprecision in the exchange was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP cooperated with the ground crew within standards, but signals were given at the moment of the action rather than before it, and the crew's position was confirmed by a quick glance rather than by a positive check. The trend is toward coordination that depends on the ground crew reacting in time. SP is expected to establish and confirm the crew's position before every switch or control movement on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: TAXI ROUTE COMPLIANCE, OBSTACLE CLEARANCE AND STOPPING THE AIRCRAFT

texts.0: SP, due to following the leader's aircraft visually without reference to the assigned taxi route, did not follow the specified taxi route and did not ensure that the ground path was clear of obstacles. SP cut the corner of the taxiway at the second turn and brought the wingtip inside the clearance margin of a parked aircraft, then stopped the aircraft with heavy oscillations. IP took the controls to stop the aircraft and reposition it on the taxiway centerline.
texts.1: SP, due to a taxi speed that remained too high for the wing clearance available in the parking area, did not ensure adequate obstacle clearance on the ground path and needed prompting to remain on the specified route. The stops at the run-up position were achieved with pronounced oscillations and only after IP called for the brakes to be released. Route and stopping technique remained at the lower limit of the standard for the whole taxi.
texts.2: SP, due to a late identification of the assigned holding point, initially began the turn toward the wrong taxiway. SP recognized the error, returned to the specified taxi route and confirmed the ground path was clear before continuing, and thereafter stopped the aircraft as required without oscillations and without IP intervention. The aircraft did not move at any point at which it was required to be halted.
texts.3: SP followed the specified taxi route throughout and ensured that the ground path of the aircraft was clear of obstacles, keeping the aircraft on the taxiway centerline behind the leader. SP stopped the aircraft as required without oscillations and without IP intervention, and did not allow any aircraft movement during the leak check and the line-up. Wingtip and jet blast clearance were maintained at all times.
texts.4: SP taxied the aircraft with exceptional precision, holding the centerline through every turn of the specified route and maintaining generous clearance from all obstacles and parked aircraft. Every stop was made smoothly at the intended point with no oscillation, and the aircraft remained completely stationary during the leak check and line-up. Deviations from the assigned route and from the intended stopping points were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP followed the taxi route and stopped the aircraft within standards, but the aircraft was consistently offset from the centerline in the turns and the stops were made with a single firm brake application rather than a progressive one. The trend is toward a taxi technique that works on a clear taxiway but reduces the clearance available in the parking area. SP is expected to track the centerline through the turns and stop the aircraft progressively on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: AIRCRAFT CONDITION ASSESSMENT AND GROUND ABORT DECISION AS A FLIGHT MEMBER

texts.0: SP, due to a determination to keep the two-ship intact after the leader had already started, did not specify the aircraft condition correctly and decided that the aircraft was permissible for flight with an indication that required a ground abort. SP did not report the discrepancy to the leader or to the ground crew and continued the start sequence. IP had to stop the sequence, declare the aircraft unserviceable and initiate the spare aircraft procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to delay the flight, assessed the aircraft condition hesitantly and reported the system indication to the leader only after IP directed it. The decision on flight permissibility was reached at the lower limit of the standard, after IP had reviewed the Flight Manual limits with SP on the interphone. The flight was held about seven minutes at the parking position while the assessment was completed.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial assessment made before the system had fully stabilized, first judged an indication to be within limits when it was not. SP rechecked the indication against the Flight Manual, corrected the assessment and passed a clear serviceability report to the leader in good time, without IP intervention. The flight's ground plan was adjusted and the sortie proceeded on the briefed timeline.
texts.3: SP specified the aircraft condition correctly and confidently and decided its flight permissibility in accordance with the Flight Manual and SOPs. The serviceability status was passed to the leader clearly and early enough for the flight to act on it. No prompting or verification by IP was required.
texts.4: SP assessed the aircraft condition to an exceptional standard, identifying a developing indication before it reached a limit, verifying it against the Flight Manual and presenting the leader with both the status and the recommended course of action. The decision on flight permissibility was made confidently and communicated in time for the flight to preserve the briefed timeline. Any imprecision in the assessment was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP assessed the aircraft condition within standards, but the decision on flight permissibility was reached slowly and was clearly influenced by the flight's departure time. The trend is toward accepting the aircraft in order to keep the two-ship together rather than on the strength of the indications. SP is expected to make and report the serviceability decision on the Flight Manual criteria alone, independently of the flight schedule, on the next sortie.
